extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, corporate communicators, and PR students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, producing, distributing, and managing television public-service announcements, PR film/featurettes, talk-show appearances, and in-house corporate video for public relations purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of television to re-create events and distribute widely
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce visually compelling recreations or features (e.g., re-creating historic rides or races) that can be distributed to many stations to generate broad coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show high pickup (e.g., a 90-second clip used by 185 stations). Aim for content that fits broadcast formats and editorial needs to maximize station usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: PSA research and testing (focus groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use focus groups to review multiple storyboards and scripts and revise based on findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Summit County example used a 15-person focus group to evaluate eight storyboards; findings led to amendments. Testing helps discover tone and content preferences (e.g., avoidance of preaching).

rubrics_metrics.name: PSA tone — avoid preaching; stimulate new thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: PSAs are most successful when they avoid preaching and instead stimulate new thinking about the issue or target group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus-group research indicated that providing opportunities for affected people to speak and using fresh language increased effectiveness for messages about mentally handicapped people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate PSAs with a complete media program
rubrics_metrics.description: Use PSAs in conjunction with talk shows, news programs, and other media outreach as part of a larger campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Summit County campaign paired PSAs with booked talk-show appearances and news coverage to achieve hours of TV exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact stations early to learn available free formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Before planning production, contact area stations to learn special formats they provide free (e.g., station-produced feature segments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stations like WNEW produce 'Big Apple Minutes' using station personalities and crews — this can save nonprofits thousands of dollars and improve placement chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–benefit assessment for television production
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully weigh expected benefits against high production and distribution costs before producing television spots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing 16-mm TV-quality film can cost $20,000–$100,000. If benefits don't justify costs, consider station-produced features, donated production, or other outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split-script preproduction format for TV spots
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a split script with full visual descriptions on the left and dialogue/narration on the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous story conferences are necessary; ensure every word in a 30- or 60-second script conveys important information and coordinate with technicians on sound, camera, actors, props, and settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor material to media needs (don't pressure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with media professionals to tailor material to the station’s format and needs rather than pressuring for placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form media consortia, visit stations, learn placement habits, and provide background material and help finding spokespeople to increase acceptance and usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background material and spokespeople to talk shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Give talk-show hosts background materials and arrange for appropriate spokespeople (including affected persons) to appear on shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assist producers in booking guests; prepare proposals and materials that make booking and on-air segments easy for producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television handout production format and quality standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare visual handouts on formats stations commonly use (three-quarter-inch videotape cassettes are increasingly standard); film PR material should be 16-mm color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tape cassettes are cheap to produce/copy and easy to mail. Super-8 and most small video formats are not considered broadcast quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background stock footage and 'handout' style
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply stations with background stock footage and adopt a 'handout' presentation (e.g., stand-up reporter) so material blends smoothly with news programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stations often prefer material that integrates with their editorial style; supplying stock footage from operations can increase pick-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-content selection — topics with higher pickup rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose topics with historically higher station usage (e.g., sports-related films, women's news, energy/technology stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A film service found average usage of supplied news films at about 45% and noted sports and technology content are in demand; tailor topics accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting on talk shows — research format and contact producers
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the target show's format, contact talent coordinators or assistant producers by phone for initial screening, and follow up with a written proposal if requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers prefer phone contact for quick screening. Be prepared to explain what makes the guest interesting; keep ideas on file for future fits (Phil Donahue example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match guest/topic to show characteristics (visual appeal, controversy, content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select shows where the guest/topic fits the show's style — some prioritize celebrities/oddities, others value consumer/serious issues or visual demonstrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some shows reward controversy or visual demonstrations; avoid heavy-handed product plugs but informal 'plugs' during broader discussions are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim feature length for broadcast slots (≈24 minutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When producing longer features intended for local broadcast, target about 24 minutes to fit within a half-hour slot and allow room for ads and announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a brochure/fact sheet with representative stills, synopsis, running time, format, and narration to promote the tape to station managers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare promotional materials for station programming decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide station managers with brochures, fact sheets, stills, and synopses to improve chances of scheduling and promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance scheduling can enable cross-promotion (local advertising, bill stuffers, house organ articles) and increase audience reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive videotaping to rebut adversarial coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticized on TV, prepare point-by-point videotaped rebuttals (defensive videotaping) for stakeholders and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Illinois Power) used a 44-minute tape to rebut claims; be mindful of copyright issues (networks may claim infringement) and legal 'fair use' arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader counter-campaigns beyond videotape
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine videotaped responses with other tactics (print ads, booklets, direct lobbying, hearings) to raise public-policy questions and influence opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kaiser used print ads and a booklet to frame debate about investigative television journalism and pressed for hearings — multi-channel strategies can amplify impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage alternative video outlets (cable public-access, playback units, public TV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use public-access cable channels, video playback units in institutions, nonprofit public television, and closed-circuit links to reach targeted audiences outside commercial networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-access channels often reserve times for community groups; public TV may be more open to innovative programming and teleconferences; placement depends on audience and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether TV reaches your target public
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether television's large audience and visual impact justify its cost based on whether the target public is in the television audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television is not the solution to every PR problem; if target publics are small or unlikely to view TV, other media may be more cost-effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate video roles and budgeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider in-house production for training, internal communications, annual reports, and conferencing — many organizations maintain studios with varied budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By the early 1980s many organizations produced large volumes of video; typical medium-sized companies budget ~ $100,000 and a small production staff; average program costs (historical) cited around $10,000.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studio physical requirements and setup
rubrics_metrics.description: Design studio space with appropriate ceiling height (12–15 ft preferred), adequate square footage (ideally ~300 sq ft), sound-absorbent materials, neutral backdrop, and basic furniture/visual-aid equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller rooms (e.g., 12x12) can work for in-house channels; use acoustic tiles or cork, velvet curtains on tracks, and provide a desk, chairs, easel, and blackboard as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Camera selection and mobile ENG capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use small-format cameras on rolling tripods for studio work and Porta-Pak/ENG units for field electronic-news-gathering to capture live, visual material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-camera setups increase visual interest; Porta-Pak units enable a crew to gather footage on location for editing back in the studio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and editing standards (electronic editing preferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use electronic editing rather than physical splicing for higher-quality assembly of scenes, sound, and superimposed titles; consider special-effects generators for transitions and overlays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic editing assembles pieces onto a master finished reel for duplication; sound mixers join narration, music, and effects onto a single soundtrack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighting and sound equipment basics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide key lighting (portable high-intensity lamps with reflectors), unidirectional lavalier microphones for speakers, omnidirectional mics for ambient sound, and a microphone switcher for multiple speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-format video can achieve acceptable quality with basic lighting and mic setups; ensure shadow control and good key lighting for faces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playback and audience-projection methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use suitcase-sized playback units and TV monitors for small groups; link monitors for larger audiences or use projection optics/large screens for big groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For audiences >10, link monitors or project to ensure visibility; glass-screen monitors give brighter, better-focused images than projection in many cases.
